TOPOLOGY

End-to-End Cloud-Native Delivery Blueprint

Separation of concerns between developer workspace, supply chain gating, and in-cluster GitOps engine

1. Developer Workspace Trunk-Based Git Push • Conventional Commits • SSH Cryptographic Signatures
↓ Webhook / CI Trigger
2. Supply Chain & Build Pipeline Hermetic Build • CycloneDX SBOM • Trivy CVE Gate • Cosign Signing
↓ Image Digest to Registry + PR to Config Repo
3. GitOps Reconciliation Engine (Argo CD) Pull-based Verification • Sync Waves • Automated Self-Healing
↓ Enforced Cluster State
4. PROEN Cloud Kubernetes Cluster Distroless Pods • PostgreSQL Locks • OpenTelemetry Observability

1. Zero Cluster Credentials in External CI

External GitHub Actions or GitLab runners never possess cluster-admin keys. The cluster maintains zero inbound open management ports.

2. Cryptographic Proof of Provenance

Every container image is signed via Cosign with verified SBOM attestations. Unsigned containers are blocked at admission.

3. Automated Drift Detection & Self-Healing

Out-of-band mutations (kubectl edit) are flagged as OutOfSync and automatically reverted to Git within seconds.

The 'Works on My Machine' Dilemma

Why heterogeneous workstations cause catastrophic delays during distributed cloud workshops

The Day 1 Engineering Nightmare

In traditional workshops and enterprise onboarding, 40% of time is wasted debugging local path discrepancies, missing CLI versions, Docker socket permissions, and outdated Helm charts.

When an engineer says "It works on my machine," they expose an uncontrolled, non-reproducible runtime environment.

Target Standard: Today we enforce a strict, standardized pre-flight audit to guarantee that all 50 participant workstations run identical, deterministic tooling.

Common Workstation Failure Points

  • Mismatched kubectl client/server API versions.
  • Docker Desktop license or credential socket lockups.
  • Git without SSH commit signing capability (< v2.34).
  • Missing OIDC token support for Cosign image attestation.

MODULE 01 | 09:00 – 09:30 ICT
THE HOOK

The Fragility of Stateful 'Pet' Servers

Why monolithic applications collapse when lifted directly into auto-scaling Kubernetes clusters

The Midnight Auto-Scale Disaster

A legacy web application is migrated to Kubernetes. At 00:00, traffic surges. The Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA) spins up 10 new Pod replicas.

Disaster strikes:

  • Users are logged out because sessions are stored in local server RAM.
  • Uploaded receipts vanish because they were saved to local /tmp.
  • When the HPA scales down, in-flight orders are aborted by sudden SIGKILL, leaving customer payments charged but tickets unissued.

The Shift from Pets to Cattle

Pets (Legacy): Servers given unique names, nurtured, manually configured, and rebooted with fear.

Cattle (Cloud-Native): Identical, disposable, stateless compute units. If one becomes unhealthy, Kubernetes terminates it instantly and provisions an identical replacement without data loss.

The Solution: The 12-Factor App methodology enforces the contract required for seamless cloud execution.

MODULE 01 | ARCHITECTURE THEORY
MAIN KNOWLEDGE

The Modern 12-Factor Contract for Kubernetes

Core architectural tenets that separate resilient cloud services from brittle legacy monoliths

FACTOR III

Config in Environment

Never bake credentials into container layers. Inject configuration via Kubernetes ConfigMap and Vault-backed Secrets.

FACTOR VI

Stateless Processes

Shared-nothing architecture. Sticky sessions are an anti-pattern. Session tokens live in JWT/Redis; media streams directly to object storage.

FACTOR IX

Disposability & Fast Boot

Services must boot in under 5 seconds and shut down gracefully upon receiving SIGTERM, draining in-flight requests without errors.

FACTOR VII

Port Binding

Export HTTP/gRPC services by binding to an assigned port. Routing and SSL termination are managed by the Ingress controller.

FACTOR XI

Logs as Event Streams

Never write log files to local disk. Emit single-line structured JSON to stdout for collection by DaemonSet agents (Loki/FluentBit).

FACTOR XII

Admin Processes

Run schema migrations as one-off Kubernetes Jobs, separated completely from continuous web-serving Pod lifecycles.

Graceful Shutdown & Health Probes Lab

Inspect and run the 12-Factor sample microservice with triple health probes and connection draining

02-sample-app/src/index.ts
// Graceful SIGTERM Signal Handler
const handleSignal = (signal: string) => {
  isShuttingDown = true;
  isReady = false; // Immediately drops from Ingress endpoints

  server.close(async () => {
    // Drain active database connections
    await dbPool.end();
    await redis.quit();
    process.exit(0);
  });

  // Safety valve: Force kill after 25s
  setTimeout(() => process.exit(1), 25000).unref();
};

process.on('SIGTERM', () => handleSignal('SIGTERM'));

Step-by-Step Lab Execution

cd workshop-setup/02-sample-app
# 1. Start local PostgreSQL + Redis + App stack (All OS)
docker compose up -d --build

# 2. Test the startup & readiness probes
# macOS / Linux / Windows curl:
curl -i http://localhost:3000/healthz/startup
curl -i http://localhost:3000/healthz/readiness

# Windows PowerShell alternative:
Invoke-RestMethod http://localhost:3000/healthz/readiness

# 3. View Prometheus metrics
curl -s http://localhost:3000/metrics | grep http_
Key Insight: When isReady = false, Kubernetes stops sending new client requests before server.close() begins draining active connections!

MODULE 01 | SUMMARY
KEY TAKEAWAYS

12-Factor Production Rules & Anti-Patterns

Architectural rules of thumb for building disposable, cloud-native microservices

Production Anti-Patterns to Avoid

  • Hardcoding credentials or embedding .env.production into Docker images.
  • Writing uploaded files to local container storage (lost on Pod restart).
  • Ignoring SIGTERM and getting killed abruptly after 30s by SIGKILL.
  • Writing logs to /var/log/app.log and configuring logrotate inside containers.

Architectural Rules of Thumb

  • Zero State: Treat every Pod as capable of disappearing at any second.
  • Probe Hygiene: Always configure distinct startup, readiness, and liveness probes.
  • Resource Envelopes: Explicitly define requests and limits for CPU and memory.
  • Structured Output: Emit unbuffered single-line JSON to stdout.

MODULE 02 | HANDS-ON PRACTICE
STEP-BY-STEP

DORA Metrics & The Blameless Postmortem Lab

Transforming outages into systemic improvements using the 5 Whys and Architecture Decision Records

The 5 Whys Root Cause Analysis (RCA)

1. Why did checkout return 500 errors?
Database connection pool was exhausted.

2. Why was the pool exhausted?
Each request spawned a new connection without releasing.

3. Why were connections not released?
Unhandled promise rejection in refund logic bypassed client.release().

4. Why was this unhandled in production?
Integration tests lacked failure-path coverage for cancelled orders.

5. Why was coverage missing?
CI lacked automated contract-testing gates.

Architecture Decision Record (ADR) Protocol

Decisions must be documented in Git alongside code:

  • Title: ADR-0012: Enforce PgBouncer Transaction Pooling
  • Context: High-concurrency ticket releases exhaust connections.
  • Decision: Deploy PgBouncer between Pods and PostgreSQL.
  • Consequences: Named prepared statements must be disabled.
Golden Rule: Blameless RCA never asks "Who made the mistake?" It asks "What system gap allowed this to happen?"

The 10:00:00 AM Ticket Rush Disaster

When vertical traffic spikes trigger overselling, deadlocks, and cascading outages

FAILURE MODE 1

Overselling & Race Conditions

500 parallel checkout requests query SELECT stock FROM tickets. All 500 read stock = 1, and all proceed to sell passes, overselling the venue by 499 seats.

FAILURE MODE 2

Cascading Thread Death

A downstream payment gateway responds in 12s instead of 200ms. Upstream microservices keep HTTP connections open, starving the entire worker pool.

FAILURE MODE 3

Cache Thundering Herd

The event layout cache key expires at 10:00:00. 10,000 concurrent users hit the primary database simultaneously to recalculate the same JSON payload.

The Mission: Implement mathematical concurrency locking, circuit breaking, and probabilistic cache stampede defense.

MODULE 03 | DISTRIBUTED SYSTEMS PATTERNS
MAIN KNOWLEDGE

Concurrency Control, Saga & Circuit Breakers

Architectural patterns for bulletproof transactional consistency during traffic surges

Pessimistic Row-Level Locking (PostgreSQL)

SELECT ... FOR UPDATE locks the specific inventory row within an ACID transaction. Concurrent transactions queue gracefully, guaranteeing that stock decrements are strictly serialized.

The Saga Pattern vs. Distributed 2PC

Two-Phase Commit does not scale across microservices. Sagas coordinate distributed business transactions through a sequence of local transactions and automated compensating transactions upon failure.

CLOSED
Normal operation; requests pass
→ Failure > 50% →
OPEN
Fail fast; zero downstream calls
→ Cooldown 30s →
HALF-OPEN
Probe traffic; auto-recovery
Circuit Breaker State: Protects payment gateways and downstream APIs from being crushed during upstream traffic surges.

await client.query('BEGIN');

// Exclusive row lock blocks concurrent checkouts
const res = await client.query(`
  SELECT total_capacity, issued_count 
  FROM ticket_tiers WHERE id = $1 FOR UPDATE;
`, [tierId]);

if (res.rows[0].issued_count >= res.rows[0].total_capacity) {
  throw new ConflictException('Sold Out');
}

await client.query(`
  UPDATE ticket_tiers 
  SET issued_count = issued_count + 1 WHERE id = $1;
`, [tierId]);

await client.query('COMMIT');

Row Locks
FOR UPDATE

Always lock inventory rows inside atomic DB transactions. Never use unconstrained UPDATE.

XFetch

MODULE 04 | 11:15 – 12:00 ICT
THE HOOK

The Trojan Horse in Your Container Image

How modern supply chain attacks compromise production clusters without breaking code

The Attack on Open-Source Dependencies

Modern applications are 90% third-party dependencies and base image layers. Attackers no longer bother penetrating outer firewalls—they poison the software supply chain:

  • Compromised base images: Official images shipped with unpatched OpenSSL/glibc CVEs.
  • Typosquatting & hijacked npm packages: Malicious code injected into popular sub-dependencies.
  • CI Runner Breaches: Attackers alter binary compilation steps (e.g., SolarWinds, Codecov).

The Zero-Trust Imperative

In a zero-trust architecture, you cannot trust a container image simply because it is stored in your private registry. You must demand cryptographic mathematical proof of:

  • Exact source commit provenance.
  • Software Bill of Materials (SBOM).
  • Cryptographic signature generated by a verified CI runner.

MODULE 04 | SUPPLY CHAIN SECURITY
MAIN KNOWLEDGE

SLSA Framework & Distroless Containerization

Reducing vulnerability attack surfaces and enforcing end-to-end provenance

SLSA 1: Build Automation Automated builds generating verifiable metadata
SLSA 2: Signed Provenance Hosted build service provides cryptographically signed attestations
SLSA 3: Isolated Ephemeral Runners Hermetic builds prevent cross-build tampering
SLSA 4: Two-Person Review & Hermetic Gating Guaranteed reproducible builds with mandatory peer sign-off

Google Distroless Strategy

Standard Linux images (Ubuntu, Debian, Alpine) include shells (/bin/sh), package managers (apt, apk), and utilities (curl, wget).

Distroless contains ONLY the application binary. If an attacker exploits an application vulnerability, there is no shell to spawn and no package manager to download secondary malware.

The Superpower of Layer Rebasing

Traditional Dockerfiles bake the OS and application together. If an OS vulnerability occurs, all 500 apps must recompile from source.

With Paketo Buildpacks, the OS layer is cleanly separated. You can swap out the vulnerable OS layer across all containers in milliseconds with pack rebase without touching code!

MODULE 06 | 13:20 – 14:00 ICT
THE HOOK

The Mystery Outage at 3:00 AM

Why unstructured text logs are utterly useless in distributed microservice architectures

The Fog of Distributed Systems

An on-call engineer receives an alert: "Checkout failure rate is 25%."

They SSH into servers and open log files. They see 10,000 lines of unformatted text per second. An error appears in the API gateway, but the actual cause was a silent timeout in the inventory service caused by a PostgreSQL lock contention.

Without distributed correlation IDs, tracing a single transaction across 5 microservices takes hours.

Observability vs. Simple Monitoring

Monitoring: Tells you that a system is broken (e.g., HTTP 500 error count > 10).

Observability: Allows you to understand why a system is broken by interrogating internal states from external telemetry outputs (Metrics, Logs, and Traces).

The Goal: Unified telemetry linked by a shared W3C trace_id across the entire PROEN Cloud infrastructure.

W3C traceparent headers propagated across network boundaries.

Progressive Canary Delivery (Argo Rollouts)

Do not deploy new code to 100% of users simultaneously. Step traffic progressively:

1 10% Traffic • Validate Error Rate for 5m

3 50% Traffic • Confirm Zero Regressions
4 100% Full Promotion • Terminate Old Pods

Canary Rollout & Prometheus Alerting Lab

Configure Argo Rollouts with automated metric analysis and Prometheus SLO alert rules

Argo Rollouts Canary Specification
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Rollout
metadata:
  name: order-service
spec:
  replicas: 10
  strategy:
    canary:
      steps:
        - setWeight: 10
        - pause: { duration: 5m }
        - setWeight: 50
        - pause: { duration: 5m }
      analysis:
        templates:
          - templateName: error-rate-check
# If error rate > 1%, automatically ABORT rollout!

Prometheus High Error Rate Rule

- alert: HighHttpErrorRate
  expr: |
    sum(rate(http_requests_total{status=~"5.."}[2m])) 
    / 
    sum(rate(http_requests_total[2m])) > 0.01
  for: 2m
  labels: { severity: critical }
  annotations:
    summary: "API Error rate exceeded 1% on {{ $labels.service }}"
Automated Rollback: If Prometheus triggers HighHttpErrorRate during Canary evaluation, Argo Rollouts instantly aborts and shifts 100% of traffic back to Stable!

The Nightmare of 'Merge Hell'

Why 3-month GitFlow feature branches destroy engineering velocity and lead to regressions

The Legacy GitFlow Trap

A development team follows traditional GitFlow: long-lived feature, develop, and release branches.

The breakdown:

  • Team A works on a checkout redesign for 6 weeks.
  • Team B refactors the database models in parallel.
  • When Team A tries to merge, they encounter 140 merge conflicts across 80 files.
  • Engineers spend 4 days resolving conflicts manually, inadvertently deleting bug fixes.

In GitOps, Git IS the Production State

In a GitOps architecture, Git is not just code storage; it is the cryptographic audit log of production infrastructure.

Sloppy Git practices—unreviewed commits, long branches, spoofed author emails—compromise the entire compliance and deployment engine.

Trunk-Based Development & Semantic Releases

Merging small, atomic increments into main daily with automated SemVer tagging

main (Trunk) Always deployable • Continuous integration • Production mirror

Conventional Commits Specification

  • feat(auth)!: replace legacy API keys with OAuth2
    → Triggers MAJOR bump (v1.2.0 → v2.0.0)

THE HOOK

The Danger of CI Cluster Credentials

Why granting Jenkins or GitHub Actions cluster-admin keys violates Zero Trust

The Push-Model Security Breach

In traditional CI/CD, developers store a kubeconfig with cluster-admin privileges inside GitHub Secrets or GitLab CI variables.

The catastrophic risk:

  • If a malicious npm package compromises a build runner, attackers steal the cluster credentials.
  • Corporate firewalls must punch inbound holes to allow external CI servers to access internal Kubernetes APIs.
  • Manual changes made directly to the cluster (kubectl edit) are never reflected back in Git.

The Pull-Model Revolution (GitOps)

The GitOps agent (Argo CD) runs inside the protected Kubernetes cluster.

  • Zero cluster credentials stored in external CI tools.
  • Outbound HTTPS read-only access to Git; zero inbound firewall ports required.
  • Continuous reconciliation guarantees that manual cluster tampering is automatically reverted.

The 4 OpenGitOps Principles (CNCF)

The formal specification governing declarative system synchronization

1

Declarative

System desired state is expressed declaratively in Kubernetes YAML / Helm / Kustomize.

2

Versioned

Desired state is stored in Git with complete revision history and immutable commit SHAs.

3

Pulled Auto

In-cluster software agents pull state automatically. No external push commands.

4

Reconciled

Continuously observes live state and automatically heals configuration drift.

"Git is the single source of truth for infrastructure and application state. What is in Git is in the cluster; what is not in Git does not exist."

Repository Separation & In-Cluster Pull Lab

Structuring application source code repositories separately from declarative GitOps config repos

Clean Separation of Repositories
REPO 1: app-source-code.git (Developers)
├── src/
├── package.json
└── Dockerfile
# Triggers CI: Runs tests, builds image, pushes digest

REPO 2: workshop-gitops.git (Argo CD)
├── base/
│   ├── deployment.yaml
│   └── service.yaml
└── overlays/
    ├── staging/
    │   └── kustomization.yaml (image: v1.3.0-rc1)
    └── production/
        └── kustomization.yaml (image: v1.2.0)
# Argo CD monitors this repo and syncs cluster

Why Repo Separation Matters

  • Prevents Infinite Loops: If CI updates deployment manifests in the same repo, it triggers a new CI build loop.
  • Least Privilege Access: Developers have commit rights to code; only automated release bots and platform leads can merge to production config.
  • Multi-Environment Promotion: Promote images across environments by updating simple Kustomize tags.

The Danger of Configuration Drift

When manual hotfixes create invisible snowflake clusters that fail during disaster recovery

The Snowflake Cluster Syndrome

During a production outage, an engineer runs:

kubectl edit deployment/order-service
# Changes memory limit from 512Mi to 2Gi manually

The immediate incident is resolved. But the change was never committed to Git.

Six months later, the cluster fails. When the cluster is rebuilt, the manual 2Gi memory patch is missing. The service crashes under normal traffic. Nobody remembers the manual hotfix.

Argo CD Automated Self-Healing

Argo CD compares live Kubernetes cluster state against the Git repository every 3 minutes (or instantly via Git webhooks).

If anyone modifies the cluster manually, Argo CD detects the divergence and overwrites it back to the Git source of truth automatically.

The Lab: We will deploy workloads, order rollouts with Sync Waves, and intentionally inject cluster drift.

Argo CD Controller Architecture

Internal component topology powering enterprise GitOps synchronization

01

API Server

Exposes gRPC/REST APIs and the Web UI. Manages authentication, RBAC policies, OIDC/Dex SSO, and audit event streams.

02

Repository Server

03

Application Controller

The core continuous reconciliation engine. Compares live cluster state against Git and triggers self-healing mutations.

The Application CRD: Binds a Git repository path (source) to a Kubernetes namespace (destination) with automated sync, prune, and self-heal policies.

MODULE 10 | 16:45 – 17:00 ICT
THE HOOK

The Plaintext Secret in Git Disaster

The #1 security blunder in enterprise GitOps adoption

The Base64 Secret Fallacy

A developer is told that GitOps requires everything to be committed to Git. They create a Kubernetes Secret:

apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
data:
  password: c3VwZXItc2VjcmV0LXBhc3N3b3Jk # base64!

The catastrophic reality: Base64 is an encoding format, NOT encryption. Anyone with read access to the Git repository decodes the database password in 1 millisecond using echo ... | base64 -d.

The Zero-Plaintext Secret Rule

Never commit unencrypted passwords, API tokens, or private keys to version control—even in private repositories.

The Enterprise Solution: Use the External Secrets Operator (ESO) to decouple secret declarations from secret values.

External Secrets Operator (ESO) & Disaster Recovery

Synchronizing secrets from enterprise Vaults and achieving 15-minute disaster recovery

↓ Authenticated Fetch

15-Minute Disaster Recovery Sequence

Because the entire desired state is stored in Git:

  • T+0: Total datacenter failure declared.
  • T+3m: Provision fresh Kubernetes cluster on PROEN Cloud.
  • T+5m: Install Argo CD operator via single Helm command.
  • T+7m: Apply root "App-of-Apps" Application manifest.
  • T+15m: All 50 microservices fully restored from Git!
